title: Bay Area Techie Dies After Valley Fever Guts His Lungs
excerpt: Chiranjeevi Kolla, 37, spent nearly a month on a ventilator in Walnut Creek before succumbing to a fungal disease most people never hear about.
body:
Chiranjeevi Kolla, a 37-year-old Indian tech professional living in Walnut Creek, California, died on May 5 after nearly a month fighting Valley fever — a soil-borne fungal infection that destroyed his lungs and left his wife and five-year-old son without their family's anchor.

**What happened:**
Kolla first fell ill in early April with what appeared to be flu-like symptoms. When his condition worsened, he sought emergency care, where doctors initially suspected severe pneumonia. Further testing later confirmed Valley fever, a fungal infection caused by inhaling microscopic spores of Coccidioides, a fungus found in soil in parts of the American Southwest, including California. He spent nearly a month in intensive care at Kaiser Permanente, where he was placed on a ventilator as doctors worked to stabilize his condition.

**Why Valley fever is so dangerous:**
Valley fever, medically known as coccidioidomycosis, is a lung infection caused by breathing in fungal spores from disturbed soil. It is not contagious from person to person. Symptoms often resemble the flu and may include cough, fever, fatigue, chest pain, and shortness of breath. In many people, the infection resolves on its own, but in some cases it can become severe, spread beyond the lungs, or cause life-threatening complications. Because patients often present with what appears to be pneumonia or bronchitis, doctors may initially prescribe antibiotics, which do not work against fungal infections. In some cases, diagnosis takes weeks. That delay can become dangerous if the infection progresses rapidly. There is currently no vaccine for Valley fever.

**The climate threat growing beneath our feet:**
His case underscores a growing public health concern in parts of the United States where climate conditions, dust exposure, and expanding development are increasing the spread of fungal diseases that often go undiagnosed in the early stages. Kolla lived in the San Francisco Bay Area with his wife, Pavani Marella, and their five-year-old son, Vihan. The family fundraiser aims to help manage hospital expenses, funeral arrangements in both the U.S. and India, childcare costs, and future educational expenses for their son.

**What to watch:**
Watch whether California public health authorities accelerate Valley fever awareness campaigns targeting immigrant and newcomer communities, and whether employers in the Bay Area tech sector begin environmental health briefings for employees relocating from overseas.
